newsitem.title: CHINA: GM confident on Shanghai target date.
newsitem.headline: GM confident on Shanghai target date.

text.p: General Motors Corp's massive investment in Shanghai has not yet received final approval but remains on schedule for the first car to roll off the assembly line by the end of 1998, a senior GM official said on Thursday.

The feasibility study for the $1 billion project was approved by China's State Council (cabinet) in January, but the final contract is still being reviewed, Philip Murtaugh, GM's chief representative in Shanghai said in an interview.
He said the delays in the approval process had not so far altered the target of beginning production in the fourth quarter of 1998.
"That's still our target. We'd like to see approval sooner rather than later to make the deadline," he said.
He said delays in approving the project, which received the initial go-ahead in October 1995, were the result of the project's complexity and the desire of Chinese officials to get it right.
"I don't think there's a problem, it's just a lengthy process," he said.

The plant will produce a middle-size luxury sedan which GM sees competing with current Chinese imports of Toyota's Lexus, Daimler-Benz's Mercedes-Benz and Bayerische Motoren Werke's BMW for use by chauffer-driven senior officials.
Murtaugh said the decision to go with a luxury car was based on GM's more negative assessment of the potential and competition in the market for small cars.
"There are well-established Chinese makes in the compact and sub-compact market, but the mid-upper luxury side is now basically an import market," he said.
Production will eventually hit around 100,000 cars a year, Murtaugh said, but he declined to give a time-scale.
For the luxury car sector GM is targeting, Murtaugh said China sales in 1996 were probably in the 100,000-120,000 range.
He discounted talk of a downturn in Chinese auto sales, saying falling sales of some vehicle types did not seem to be affecting the sedan car market.

"This is one of the fastest growing markets in the world for cars," he said. "People talk about how last year was such a disastrous year, but sales of sedan cars grew by 20 percent last year. If that's a disaster, then the U.S. would love to see that kind of a disaster."
He said he expected to see overall car sales in China rise in line with the overall growth in the economy.
Murtaugh said GM's target was for the plant, to be built in the Pudong development zone east of Shanghai's city centre, to move into profit within five years.
"We wouldn't be getting into this if it was a charitable situation," he said.
He said production costs in China were higher than in the United States due to the less well-developed infrastructure, higher raw materials costs and the general cost of doing business.
Exports from the plant are planned at around 15-20 percent of output "depending on the ability to meet quality and price requirements in world markets", he said.
Any exports would go to Southeast Asia, parts of the former Soviet Union or Europe, he said, adding: "We do not foresee exporting to North America."
